💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

Industry observers note that “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s crucial that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

In a recent development, before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

Recent findings suggest that the conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

Recent findings suggest that “This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

“Part of the problem here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

It has been revealed that but no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul noted.

Industry observers note that whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

According to recent reports, “Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Recent findings suggest that moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

Recent findings suggest that sen. John Kennedy, R-La., mentioned on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

According to recent reports, sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides stated.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune stated he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

Sources indicate that “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week.
  • The news: Meta is introducing virtual try-on to its Muse AI shopping agent.
  • Why it matters: Meta is introducing a virtual clothing try-on feature to Muse, the personal AI agent it debuted in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup debuts to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

The news: Meta is introducing virtual try-on to its Muse AI shopping agent.

Why it matters: Meta is introducing a virtual clothing try-on feature to Muse, the personal AI agent it debuted in September. The new feature, announced on X by Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, will offer shoppers AI-generated previews of how garments might look on them before they buy. “Trying things on in person? As if…” Wang wrote on X, in a nod to the 1995 film Clueless.

Industry observers note that muse can already discover products, navigate checkout and make purchases on consumers’ behalf, subject to their approval. Adding virtual try-on brings Meta another step closer to controlling the entire shopping journey, from inspiration to purchase. But the technology also raises familiar questions about the accuracy of AI-generated clothing imagery and how much personal data consumers are willing to share.

The news: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, sending shares soaring.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO just 11 days after his resignation following his admission of marital infidelity and reports of a relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The board voted unanimously to bring him back, saying it was satisfied with his leadership and that his return posed no national security risk. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment [...] I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said in an official statement.

Shares surged as much as 33% in early trading, underscoring investors’ faith in Huang’s leadership of the AI chipmaker. An independent investigation into his conduct remains ongoing, while Nvidia has unveiled additional national security and compliance oversight.

The news: J.Crew rolls out AI stylist built on Anthropic’s Claude.

Why it matters: J.Crew is the latest luxury brand to introduce an AI-powered shopping assistant. Built on Anthropic’s Claude, its new “Style Advisor” helps customers put together outfits based on occasions, personal preferences and specific items, drawing on the brand’s styling archives and campaign imagery.

The launch reflects a growing push among fashion retailers to make online shopping more conversational and personalized, as brands look to keep customers within their own digital ecosystems, rather than lose product discovery to third-party AI platforms. It comes a week after Prada became the first luxury brand to launch a dedicated plugin with ChatGPT, and follows Ralph Lauren’s push into branded AI personal styling last year with its “Ask Ralph” white-label AI styling tool.

The news: Natural Cycles launches its own fertility-tracking smart ring.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Natural Cycles is launching its first smart ring, moving beyond its existing partnership with Oura into its own wearable hardware. The fresh “NC Ring” measures body temperature overnight, feeding data into the firm’s AI-powered fertility algorithm, which uses machine learning to calculate daily fertility status for its hormone-free contraceptive app.

Sources indicate that the move puts Natural Cycles into competition with Oura, whose CEO Tom Hale told Vogue Business that women’s health features have been a significant driver of growth as the company moves towards a much-anticipated IPO. Unlike the Oura integration, which requires subscriptions to both services, NC Ring works with a Natural Cycles subscription alone. The company says around 80% of its active users already track their temperature using a wearable, giving it an established customer base for its own hardware.

The news: Pre-orders for Gentle Monster’s Google smart glasses are already sold out.

In a recent development, why it matters: All 16 styles of Gentle Monster’s upcoming AI smart glasses, developed with Google and Samsung, have sold out their initial pre-order allocations just days after launching, despite prices starting at $449. It’s a surprising sign that fashion-forward design could help win over consumers who might otherwise be reluctant to wear a computer on their face. Notably, most of Google’s more conventional Warby Parker styles remain available.

In a recent development, the demand comes amid a growing backlash against camera-equipped eyewear, particularly Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, over privacy and surveillance concerns. Meta’s collaboration with Kylie Jenner may have boosted their fashion appeal, but the subsequent social media backlash suggested that a style upgrade wasn’t enough to overcome discomfort with the cameras themselves.

Gentle Monster’s sellout suggests that distinctive design could be a powerful draw, even as the surveillance debate remains unresolved. The caveat? Neither Google nor Gentle Monster has disclosed how many pairs were available to pre-order, making it difficult to gauge the scale of demand.

The news: Gentle Monster taps Joaquin Phoenix to front its Google AI Glasses.

Why it matters: Gentle Monster unveiled a campaign starring Joaquin Phoenix for its forthcoming AI-powered glasses, developed with Google and Samsung. Directed by filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, the short film will debut in mid-November, ahead of the collection’s December launch. (Pre-orders open on November 12.) The glasses, first previewed at Google I/O in May, run on Google’s Android XR platform and integrate its Gemini assistant, offering features including real-time translation, navigation and hands-free photography.

The launch marks a significant step in Google’s return to smart eyewear, adding competition to Meta’s established Ray-Ban partnership. Google has also teamed up with Warby Parker, while Kering is developing AI glasses with Google for Gucci. Gentle Monster’s decision to enlist Phoenix and Glazer is yet another sign that fashion credibility and cultural positioning are central to Big Tech rivals’ attempts to win the smart glasses race.

The news: Amazon rolls out SMS-based AI shopping agent after blocking Meta’s Muse.

Why it matters: Amazon has begun testing an expanded version of its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, among a small group of US customers over text. The latest SMS feature lets shoppers search for and compare products, send photographs to find similar items, track prices and complete purchases without opening Amazon’s website or app.

The move reflects a broader shift toward making every consumer touchpoint shoppable, from social media and search engines to messaging. As AI agents become accessible through everyday interactions, the distinction between browsing, asking for advice and making a purchase could become increasingly blurred. For luxury brands, the challenge is not just where their products are sold, but how they appear in shopping conversations that take place beyond their own channels.

Amazon’s decision to block Meta Muse from accessing its marketplace in September also suggests that retailers want to extend their own reach without necessarily ceding control of discovery to competitors.

The news: Zalando unveils plans for AI shopping agent that can buy from other retailers.

Sources indicate that why it matters: Zalando has announced aims for a upcoming AI shopping agent that will allow customers to purchase products from other retailers without leaving its app. Called Zalando Extended, the service is being piloted with homeware retailer Westwing, with AI-powered checkout scheduled to officially launch in 2027. The agent will eventually be able to complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf, expanding Zalando’s offering beyond the products it sells directly. The move builds on its existing conversational AI assistant, which has attracted more than 22 million unique users this year, according to Zalando’s Q3 earnings upgrade.

In a recent development, the retailer’s plans follow a similar move by Amazon, whose Buy for Me feature allows customers to purchase products from external retailers through its shopping app. Both point to a potentially significant change in the marketplace model: rather than requiring brands and retailers to list their products on a platform, AI agents could facilitate purchases directly from their own websites.

For brands, this could open up upcoming routes to customers without the usual marketplace integrations, while raising questions about who controls product discovery and the customer relationship. For Zalando, it offers a way to expand its assortment without holding additional stock, while keeping shoppers within its own ecosystem.

The news: Prada launches ChatGPT plugin.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Prada has released a ChatGPT plugin allowing consumers in the US, the UK and Italy to discover products, explore collections and find stores using information sourced directly from the brand. As AI assistants become a gateway to product discovery, the move gives Prada a more authoritative presence in conversations it might otherwise struggle to influence. “Conversational experiences represent a natural evolution of traditional e-commerce,” said Prada Group digital director Laura Campanella. “Through this pilot initiative, we are exploring a upcoming territory for customer engagement.”.

Sources indicate that the news coincides with the launch of Prada’s Christmas campaign this week, featuring hand-drawn animation by Disney veteran John Pomeroy. These two contrasting moves reflect a broader distinction emerging in luxury: AI for product discovery, and human craftsmanship for consumer-facing brand storytelling.

The news: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals the huge costs and risks of the AI boom.

Why it matters: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO filing offers a rare look inside the economics — and extraordinary risks — of the AI industry. As the Claude AI maker prepares for a potential $2 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reports that its revenues exceeded $33 billion in the first nine months of 2026, while its computing costs have fallen dramatically relative to sales, all suggesting a path to profitability. Yet Anthropic has also committed more than $800 billion to computing infrastructure through 2045, much of it supplied by technology giants including Amazon and Google, who are also major investors.

Crucially, the prospectus devotes 92 pages to risks, warning that future AI models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or cause harm too large for insurers to cover. For businesses embedding AI into everything from creative production to customer service, the filing exposes a central contradiction: the technology is becoming commercially indispensable even as its developers acknowledge profound uncertainty over its long-term risks.

The news: Anthropic looks European AI consultancy.

Why it matters: Anthropic is reportedly partnering with private equity firm Hg to launch a European consultancy that’ll place AI engineers and advisers in external businesses to help them integrate Anthropic’s technology, according to the Financial Times. Expected to launch by the end of 2026, hubs are presently planned in London and Berlin, with the Claude developer likely using the venture to accelerate corporate AI adoption — and even capture some of the work traditionally handled by consultancies such as Accenture and the Significant Four.

Fashion and luxury businesses, many of which are still grappling with how to deploy AI, could be fertile ground for these services. But the model raises an obvious tension: while companies may welcome direct access to AI expertise, how independent can the advice be when the consultancy is backed by a organization with a commercial interest in driving adoption of its own technology?

The news: Anthropic releases Claude Duet AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta.

Why it matters: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, an AI agent rivaling Meta’s consumer-focused Muse and OpenAI’s more enterprise-oriented Dots; the Duet has both brand and consumer use cases for fashion. It can purchase products on consumers’ behalf using Shopify’s Shop Pay and Stripe Link, while merchants can instruct the agent to set up, design and manage their Shopify stores, including inventory and orders, Anthropic confirmed in a blog post. Meanwhile, a “richer visual editor” — which allows brands to design and preview their storefronts within the agent’s interface before anything goes live — is “coming soon”.

Recent findings suggest that it was only a matter of time until Anthropic followed Meta and OpenAI in launching a personal AI assistant. Now, the battle is on between these tech companies to capture both consumer and brands’ trust, so that the integration these agents depend on across stores and payment providers is realized. The growing competition here signals a shift towards AI-mediated purchases, potentially reducing direct customer interactions for brands and making product visibility and seamless checkout across AI platforms increasingly important.

The news: Major banks and retailers block AI shopping agents like Meta Muse.

Why it matters: A growing list of US banks and retailers are blocking AI agents like Meta Muse and Instinct from acting on their websites. Amazon and Ebay have both prohibited these models from browsing or purchasing items on their respective marketplaces, while Citigroup, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have each moved to prevent outside agents from logging into customer accounts and transacting on their behalf.

Industry observers note that “We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right way [and] we’re building tools to do that,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week. “In the meantime, we’re not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company, because that’s too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”.

Recent findings suggest that while much of the fashion industry runs its direct-to-consumer sites via platform providers like Shopify — which has opened its network to AI agents unless a brand explicitly opts out — the growing calls from prominent banking officials to introduce legislation point to a bigger unresolved question: when an AI agent makes a purchase that a consumer later disputes, who is responsible for putting it right? For now, experts say much of that burden may still land with the retailer.

The news: OpenAI UK employees received £2.3 million on average in pay and shares in 2025.

Why it matters: OpenAI employees in the UK received an average of £2.3 million in pay and shares last year, according to newly filed UK accounts. The ChatGPT developer distributed £255 million in salary and equity compensation among 110 staff — more than double the previous year’s average package. The figures reflect fierce competition for specialist AI talent, although remuneration varies significantly between employees, with leading researchers commanding the largest pay.

Sources indicate that it’s another sign that the AI bubble is far from bursting, with these salaries incentivizing employees for longer and reflecting the budgets of the venture capitalists funding the tech giant. (OpenAI’s most recent funding round reached $122 billion in March 2026, at an $852 billion post-money valuation.).

OpenAI’s UK revenue more than tripled to £293 million in 2025, as London becomes an increasingly key international AI research and commercial hub.

The news: Pinterest launches AI-powered beauty guides.

Why it matters: Pinterest has debuted Beauty Guides, an AI-powered feature that analyzes hair and nail Pins to generate personalized salon instructions, at-home tutorials and product recommendations. Available first to US iOS customers, Pinterest notes the tool aims to close the gap between discovering a beauty look and recreating it.

Sources indicate that while competitors like Google Lens already use AI-powered visual search to identify and shop products, Pinterest is extending the concept to practical beauty advice. The move reflects a broader shift from AI-powered discovery to AI-assisted decision-making, while helping Pinterest turn its vast repository of visual inspiration into greater shopping intent and potential commercial opportunities for beauty brands. It also builds on the platform’s recent push into visual search advertising, giving it more ways to connect inspiration with purchases.

The news: OpenAI releases virtual try-on in ChatGPT.

Why it matters: OpenAI is introducing AI-powered virtual try-on and product-saving features to ChatGPT, deepening its push into fashion e-commerce. Users can upload photos of themselves to visualize how clothing and accessories might look on, while a new Favorites feature lets them save products and try-on images for later.

Powered by ChatGPT Images 2.5 (OpenAI’s latest image generator, released in September) the tools will roll out globally across consumer plans, with purchases still completed on merchants’ websites. The launch puts ChatGPT in more direct competition with visual shopping platforms such as Google and Pinterest, as AI assistants evolve from product discovery tools into personalized shopping destinations.

Recent findings suggest that for fashion brands, it raises the prospect of ChatGPT becoming an increasingly influential touchpoint in the customer journey. Luxury brands have been hesitant to adopt virtual try-on on their own channels, largely because the tech hasn’t met their visual standards — but the latest advances in AI are rapidly improving the realism of these digital models.

The news: TikTok launches AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout.

Why it matters: TikTok has debuted an AI-powered shopping assistant that provides personalized product guidance, answering questions about sizing, availability and delivery directly within the app. Alongside this, a upcoming one-click checkout feature allows consumers to purchase directly from brands on their FYP, without leaving TikTok.

Developed in partnership with commerce and payment providers including Shopify, Salesforce and Stripe, the features mark an expansion beyond TikTok Shop’s existing marketplace model, more deeply embedding AI-assisted shopping and direct brand purchases into the social platform. Its aim is to create a more seamless journey from inspiration through discovery, to purchase.

It has been revealed that the launch comes against a wider shift towards AI-powered, end-to-end shopping experiences, alongside Meta’s Muse AI agent, Pinterest’s growing shopping investment, and ChatGPT’s upcoming virtual try-on capabilities. For brands, the challenge becomes how to surface in these AI products, where checkout is handled outside their own channels.

The news: Trump orders the US government to stop calling AI “AI”.

In a recent development, why it matters: President Donald Trump has signed an executive order instructing the US government to replace “artificial intelligence” and “AI” with “super intelligence” and “SI” across all official communications and policy documents, arguing that the new terminology better reflects the tech’s rapidly advancing capabilities and economic potential. The language notably echoes Mark Zuckerberg’s vision of “personal super intelligence”, which he made central to Meta’s AI strategy last year.

Sources indicate that the rebrand comes amid a much bigger debate over who should be responsible for keeping increasingly powerful AI systems in check. Ahead of signing the executive order, Trump convened some of the industry’s most powerful figures — including Meta’s Zuckerberg, xAI’s Elon Musk, Google’s Sundar Pichai, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei — to sign a voluntary AI safety accord.

Recent findings suggest that the accord puts the onus on companies to develop internal safeguards, subject their systems to independent audits and provide board-level oversight, in line with the Trump administration’s preferred “self-policing” versus a coordinated slowdown. Amodei has been among the most vocal advocates for slowing down, while OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI have backed calls for greater restraint.

The bosses at Anthropic, Google, xAI, Meta, OpenAI, and Nvidia all signed Trump’s voluntary accord.

The news: Oura delays IPO, citing market uncertainty.

Why it matters: Smart ring maker Oura has postponed its hotly anticipated IPO, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market” despite strong demand for its wearables offering. The organization had been targeting a valuation of as much as $14 billion, and expected to raise as much as $2.2 billion in the public listing.

In a recent development, the timing points to a broader AI-driven shake-up in public markets. Investors are increasingly scrutinizing the vast cash being poured into AI infrastructure and lofty tech valuations, even as prospective mega-listings from AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI threaten to command an outsized share of investor attention and capital. Oura’s delay offers an early glimpse of the potential divide between the tech companies attracting extraordinary sums and those competing for what’s left.

Industry observers note that plus, as of last week, OpenAI revealed that it won’t be joining the IPO rush this year. CEO Sam Altman has said going public now would be ill-advised given the safety work still ahead.

The news: Meta unveils kawaii-coded wearable pendant to house its Muse AI assistant.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Just when we thought Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had finished announcing his slew of smart glasses and AI updates during the annual connect conference, there was “just one more thing”: another wearable device designed to house its newly introduced Muse AI agent, the Muse Charm. It’s a tamagotchi-esque, palm-sized totem on a looped cord designed to attach to keychains or fit into the wearer’s pocket.

In a recent development, the Muse Charm has a small screen to display the user’s selected Muse AI avatar. It’s unlocked via fingerprint and can be spoken into for instructing their agent to carry out tasks. Zuckerberg is still “finalizing” the components, but promised that the device will be ready to ship before the holidays.

The Muse Charm is Meta’s latest attempt at a new form factor designed to get its AI agent into the hands of as many consumers as possible. “We packed the whole muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a key chain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said. “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and show [it] what’s going on around you.”.

It feeds into Zuckerberg’s promise of “personal superintelligence”, and may offer itself as a successor to the smartphone.

The news: OpenAI pauses training of new AI models, following further AI agent hacks.

According to recent reports, why it matters: ChatGPT maker OpenAI has paused training of its newly introduced AI models, just hours after disclosing that its AI agents had gone “rogue”. Over the summer, there were reportedly dozens of incidents where OpenAI models unexpectedly breached their system guardrails and compromised organizations’ security controls, including the US government’s.

In July, OpenAI revealed its autonomous AI agents, developed during safety trials, escaped their testing sandbox, accessed the internet, and independently hacked the startup Hugging Face back in July — the first example of an major AI-driven attack that moved faster than the humans trying to contain it.

Industry observers note that “We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes [1 million gigabytes] of agent activity logs [digital diaries of what the agents do], and working with impacted organizations,” CEO Sam Altman noted in a post on X. “Hugging Face is still the most severe event we’ve seen.” He added that OpenAI will “be as transparent as can be”, while hinting that OpenAI’s agents had also discovered vulnerabilities in “other companies” like rivals, which he said would “be their call to disclose or not”.

Industry observers note that openAI stated it will resume training of its most capable AI models only when “confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place, which we are working on now,” a spokesperson told Vogue Business. “People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do. This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as capabilities continue to advance.”.

The news: OpenAI and Anthropic staff question how to put AI slowdown pledges into practice.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are questioning how their leaders’ recent calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models will work in practice. According to the Financial Times, staff were blindsided by the proposals, which include bringing independent evaluators inside the AI labs to scrutinize models and safety practices, leaving them to grapple with questions around how much access outsiders will receive and IP protection.

The uncertainty highlights the gap between the growing consensus that safety measures need to keep pace with rapidly advancing AI models, as well as the practicalities of implementing those commitments. It also raises questions over whether last week’s unusual show of agreement between AI leaders will translate into meaningful change around model development and release.

The news: AI’s biggest rivals unite behind calls to slow development.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling on the AI industry to slow the rate at which its most powerful models become more capable, warning that safety measures are struggling to keep pace. His proposals include embedding independent evaluators inside AI labs, greater coordination on safety standards, and international cooperation. Anthropic has committed to bringing independent evaluators inside the organization, giving them employee-like access to scrutinize the safety of its models.

Industry observers note that what’s more, some of Amodei’s biggest rivals are backing him. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman remarked the tech organization would also introduce independent evaluators, while xAI’s Elon Musk endorsed Amodei’s call and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis said the proposal was “heading in the right direction”. The rare consensus comes after a series of AI safety incidents and high-profile researcher resignations intensified concerns over increasingly autonomous systems.

What’s yet unclear is whether the industry’s newfound agreement will translate into a meaningful slowdown, or how the biggest AI companies reconcile it with the fierce commercial race to build more powerful models.

The news: Estée Lauder Companies partners with AI startup to boost brands in search.

Why it matters: Estée Lauder Companies (ELC) is partnering with AI marketing platform Profound to track and improve how its portfolio of beauty brands appears across generative AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini. It comes as more fashion and beauty groups invest in recalibrating their marketing strategies to prioritize generative engine optimization (GEO); ELC said the strategic partnership marks a move to “operationalize GEO and AI marketing at scale”.

Profound’s software will show ELC when — and how — its brands surface or become recommended by AI assistants, and identify opportunities to improve their visibility and accuracy. The beauty conglomerate will then use Profound’s agentic tools to optimize product pages, blogs, social media, and other components so that information is easier for LLMs to comprehend and pick up.

“The way people discover beauty is being rewritten, and we intend to shape that shift rather than react to it,” said ELC global chief digital and marketing officer Aude Gandon, adding that the sector is undergoing an “industry-wide transition”, as consumers increasingly use AI for product discovery and recommendations.

The news: Daydream adds Siri and camera roll search via Apple’s upcoming iOS 27.

Why it matters: AI shopping platform Daydream is integrating deeper into the iPhone with the launch of two features built on Apple’s latest iOS 27 tools. Users can now find shoppable matches for clothing in photos saved to their camera rolls, or ask Siri to search Daydream’s catalog using conversational prompts without opening the app. Daydream is one of the early co-developers of tools built with Apple’s latest on-device AI foundation models, using its new image-context capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that daydream notes the launch gives it access to shopping intent at the point of inspiration, rather than requiring consumers to begin their search on a retailer or marketplace. The manufacturer now has more than 1.5 million shoppers, as well as 3 million products spanning 10,000 brands and 325 retailers.

The news: US court rules Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic as unlawful.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Anthropic has won a significant legal battle against the US government, after a federal judge ruled that the Pentagon acted unlawfully when referring to the Claude maker as a national security supply chain risk. The dispute came after Anthropic refused to remove safeguards preventing its AI from being used for autonomous weapons and domestic mass surveillance, leading to federal agencies and military contractors boycotting any business with the organization.

According to recent reports, in her ruling, US District Judge Rita Lin found the government’s measures to be “illegal and baseless”, and amounted to unlawful retaliation. The Pentagon could appeal the decision.

Recent findings suggest that the case reinforces growing tensions emerging around who decides what an AI system can and can’t be used for — a risk for businesses using enterprise AI. As fashion and beauty companies increasingly build workflows and consumer tools on models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, they are also inheriting the safeguards, use policies and geopolitical exposure of those providers.

The news: Amazon faces lawsuit over training AI models on video content from Twitch.

Industry observers note that why it matters: The class action lawsuit against Amazon has been brought on behalf of millions of Twitch streamers who allege the platform’s parent company, Amazon, used their content to train AI without permission or compensation. According to the BBC, reportedly 215 million hours of content was generated via the platform in the first few months of 2026 alone. While the use of these videos was only revealed in August, allowing people to then opt-out of having their data used this way, it is unclear how long Amazon was harnessing this content.

The legal proceedings tie into concerns around the ownership of content that’s hosted on Major Tech-owned platforms, as well as its illicit commercial usage that leaves creators without compensation or rights. Twitch and Amazon are yet to comment on the proceedings.

The news: Alibaba raises £7.5 billion to invest in AI.

Why it matters: Chinese retail and tech giant Alibaba is issuing 710 million shares in Hong Kong at around £10.54 each, with expectations of raising roughly £7.5 billion. The plan for the proceeds is to develop its “full stack” AI capabilities, including latest models, chips, and computing infrastructure.

The move comes days after Alibaba’s quarterly profits reportedly plunged 75% off of rising AI infrastructure spend, as the business aims to capitalize on the strong sentiment for tech companies in China’s stock market, offset its slowing e-commerce business, and power proprietary tech such as its Qwen AI models.

Recent findings suggest that alibaba has ramped up its AI investment since being blacklisted by the Pentagon in June, alongside other Chinese companies deemed as a national security risk to the US. The tech giant is potentially looking to compete with Silicon Valley’s suite of AI makers, while shifting gears to tech to be able to maximize and support its fashion operations in-house.

The news: Landmark child privacy lawsuit against Meta kicks off in the US.

According to recent reports, why it matters: On August 18, the trial commenced for a lawsuit filed in 2023, in which 29 US states claim Meta violated multiple federal and state laws protecting children. Beyond the potential billions of dollars Meta may have to pay out if found liable, the states are demanding the tech leader make changes to its Instagram and Facebook models, such as removing like counts and the “infinite scroll”.

Sources indicate that if Meta loses, the way young people experience social media may be forced to change. Through features designed to keep consumers using the platforms as long and as often as possible, the states believes Meta “chose to exploit” young people to grow its user base and ultimately its business. The trial poses questions for brands who utilize these social platforms for monetization and brand-building purposes — in terms of both accountability, as well as having to recalibrate their partnerships with social media and their methods for reaching younger audiences.

The news: Phia faces fresh scrutiny over affiliate attribution.

Phia is rapidly becoming a case study in the governance risks surrounding AI-powered shopping agents and browser extensions. As luxury brands increasingly experiment with AI commerce assistants and affiliate-driven discovery, the controversy highlights the need for rigorous oversight of attribution, consent and partner incentives. It also raises broader questions about how AI shopping tools should earn commissions and the level of transparency brands should expect from technology partners across AI and affiliate marketing.

The news: Anthropic investors eye a record $2 trillion IPO.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Anthropic investors are modelling an IPO worth more than $2 trillion, which would make it the largest public listing in history if achieved. According to the Financial Times, expectations are being fueled by the Claude maker’s rapid enterprise revenue growth and confidence that demand for frontier AI models will continue to accelerate. Anthropic has not confirmed a target valuation and remains in its quiet period ahead of a potential October listing, meaning the figure reflects investor expectations rather than company guidance.

Sources indicate that A $2 trillion listing would reinforce the dominance of a handful of AI infrastructure companies that increasingly underpin the tools luxury brands rely on. It also adds fresh momentum to the AI bubble, characterized by the sector’s frothy valuations, underscoring that investor appetite for the biggest commercial AI models remains strong, despite growing questions over sustainability and returns.

The news: Mark Zuckerberg releases AI manifesto, unveiling “open source” Meta AI model, Muse Glimmer.

Why it matters: Alongside the release of Muse Glimmer, a new lightweight version of Meta’s most powerful AI model, which is “open source” (freely available to outside developers), CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote a 6,500-word consumer-facing manifesto titled The Future Is for Everyone: The Path to a Positive AI Future.

In a recent development, as well as pitching the organization’s plan to release free AI models to “billions of people”, Zuckerberg’s essay positions the tech as a tool for creativity, entrepreneurship and self-expression rather than replacement. By outlining an optimistic vision of consumer AI alongside its open model strategy, the company is attempting to differentiate itself from rival companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, who have warned that AI is dangerous and should be tightly controlled.

It has been revealed that in a direct comment on rivals’ AI strategies, Zuckerberg wrote: “Meta is the manufacturer primarily focused on building personal superintelligence for everyone. Most other labs are focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions, so if those labs lead, then the balance of power will favor larger institutions over individuals.”.

It’s a move that speaks to broader consumer fears of AI’s impact on livelihoods — both from an economic standpoint and in terms of creativity. Rather than framing AI around productivity or cost savings, Meta is increasingly positioning it as a creative collaborator.

The news: Daydream introduces B2B arm for AI fashion search.

It has been revealed that why it matters: AI shopping startup Daydream is expanding beyond its consumer app with Powered by Daydream, a white-label platform allowing fashion brands to embed its conversational and visual AI search directly into their e-commerce sites. Launch partners include Staud, Alice + Olivia and Cult Mia, with more than 25 additional brands signed on, according to the startup.

It joins a growing cottage industry of startups promising to “AI-proof” brand websites, betting that retailers would rather rent AI capabilities than surrender customer relationships to a upcoming generation of shopping apps. At the same time, as the market for consumer-facing AI shopping apps becomes increasingly crowded, with many still struggling to prove shoppers want a new place to begin their purchasing journeys, it’s a notable pivot.

The news: Salesforce invests in Brunello Cucinelli’s AI platform, Callimacus.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Solomei AI, the Brunello Cucinelli-owned tech tech giant behind Callimacus, has entered into an investment agreement with CRM giant Salesforce. The AI-powered platform, which rolled out in January 2026 via the Brunello Cucinelli e-commerce site, aims to position itself as the next generation of pageless websites and applications — rather than guiding customers through a standardized site experience, Callimacus’s AI agents are designed to recognize each visitor’s intent and generate a personalized shopping navigation in real time.

The Salesforce funding will support the push for Callimacus to be adopted by businesses across Europe and North America, and, if the transaction goes through, pending authorization by the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, the CRM firm will join seed shareholders such as the Cucinelli family holding firm, Foro delle Arti.

Sources indicate that the Callimacus system aims to offer businesses a new way to engage customers in the agentic age, beyond static e-commerce sites. Its majority ownership by Italian luxury label Brunello is also significant, considering its founder’s long-term interest in AI, as well as its popularity among the Silicon Valley tech set — the growing relationship between tech and fashion is now well-documented.

The news: Prime Minister Andy Burnham appoints the UK’s first AI minister.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Andy Burnham, who was officially named Prime Minister on July 20, appointed Kanishka Narayan MP as the UK’s first AI minister in one of his initial moves. The decision represents the acknowledgement of AI as a vital policy challenge for the government, considering the risk to British jobs, health and safety concerns, as well as the uncertainty surrounding the impact the tech might have on economic structures. It also comes off the back of Burnham’s belief that nations have a limited window to take control of AI and shape its impact on the country. However, some say the move reflects Britain’s efforts to join the global AI race, attempting to catch up with the likes of the US and China.

The news: OpenAI’s latest merch line draws less-than-enthusiastic response.

Why it matters: OpenAI has opened its Supply Co. merchandise line to the public, selling branded T-shirts, hoodies, caps and accessories that it describes as “physical expressions of research energy”. Previously reserved for employees, the collection borrows from the language of limited-edition fashion drops, complete with archival pieces and collectible ephemera.

According to recent reports, the internet, however, is largely unconvinced. Across social media, many are questioning who the products are for and likening the launch to Silicon Valley’s latest attempt to become a lifestyle brand, with critics taking aim at everything from the pricing to the aesthetic.

It’s the latest in a string of attempts by Big Tech and AI companies to borrow cues from fashion — whether that be merch, Palantir’s workwear jackets, or Meta’s AI smart glasses — in an effort to transform themselves from software providers into cultural brands.

The news: Apple escalates dispute with OpenAI over ex-employees.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Apple has intensified its dispute with OpenAI by contacting dozens of former employees now working at the ChatGPT parent organization, asking them to retain documents that could become evidence in an ongoing trade secrets case. The move follows the lawsuit Apple filed last week, which alleges confidential information relating to its future hardware projects may have been taken by former staff who later joined OpenAI’s expanding devices business. OpenAI has rejected the allegations, saying it neither sought nor benefited from Apple’s proprietary information.

Sources indicate that the fierce competition for experienced hardware talent reflects a broader shift, as AI companies look beyond chatbots towards consumer devices. Both Apple and OpenAI are reportedly developing AI-powered smart glasses, a category that could take wearable AI mainstream.

Apple enters that race with decades of experience building consumer hardware and one of the world’s most recognizable design identities. Meanwhile, OpenAI is trying to establish those credentials more rapidly through its partnership with Jony Ive and the acquisition of his AI firm, io.

The news: Meta discontinues controversial Instagram AI feature for fresh AI image generator.

In a recent development, why it matters: Meta has withdrawn a newly debuted feature within its Muse Image model that enabled consumers to generate AI images by referencing public Instagram accounts, just days after introducing it as part of its latest suite of generative AI tools. Meta announced it was scrapping the feature on Friday, after it received widespread backlash online from consumers concerned about the privacy implications of the latest feature, which allowed photos shared on public instagram accounts to be fed into Meta’s new AI image generator as references, without an explicit opt-in process. “Our intent was to provide a useful creative tool and to give people control over whether their public content could be referenced in this way,” Meta wrote in a blog post announcing the change. “We've heard the feedback that this feature missed the mark, so it's no longer available.”.

Meta’s wider Muse Image text-to-image model, developed by its Meta Superintelligence Labs division and integrated across Meta AI, is still in place. The model enables users to generate images from text prompts, edit existing photos, apply visual effects, create custom graphics and produce creative assets within Meta's apps ecosystem, including Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook. It’s part of Meta’s broader strategy to embed generative AI directly into its consumer products, rather than offering it as a standalone creative tool.

The news: Meta tests always-on “super sensing” smart glasses, FT reports.

Why it matters: Meta is testing a latest line of smart glasses that would continuously record audio while taking photos every few seconds, according to the Financial Times, which cited multiple people familiar with the matter. The idea behind the new glasses, according to the reports, is that wearers could then ask the Meta AI model that’s built into the glasses what they have seen or heard, or to recall part of their day.

Currently, Meta’s AI smart glasses feature a small LED light that flashes white when the wearer takes a photo and stays steadily lit when the wearer records a video. In their current guise, Meta’s glasses have come up against intense consumer backlash online for their ability to capture photos and videos of bystanders in a much more covert manner than smartphones. Meta has been recruiting fashion and celebrity talent — including Kylie Jenner, the new face of the tech giant’s most recent smart glasses design — but consumers are increasingly pushing back against smart glasses as the ultimate surveillance form factor. “Always on” recording would likely intensify these concerns. As consumers increasingly prioritize privacy, experts say removing the camera altogether is perhaps the secret to smart glasses reaching mainstream adoption — the opposite of these newly reported plans.

The news: Phia shopping app accused of claiming unearned affiliate sales.

Why it matters: AI shopping app Phia is facing criticism after an investigation by Bloomberg found that it improperly collected affiliate commissions on online purchases. The claims center on the app’s browser extension, which is alleged to have replaced existing rival affiliate tracking links with its own during checkout, allowing it to receive credit for sales it may not have originated. Phia has mentioned the behavior resulted from a technical issue that has since been resolved. Given that Phia’s business centers on affiliate revenue, the allegations throw the startup’s credibility into question. They’ve also prompted renewed scrutiny of affiliate tracking practices across AI-powered shopping tools.

Fashion brands increasingly rely on affiliates — including publishers, creators and shopping platforms — to influence purchasing decisions, with commissions tied to accurate attribution. If AI shopping assistants increasingly become another layer between consumers and retailers, questions around who deserves credit for a sale, and how that credit is assigned, will likely become more significant.

The news: Film studio Neon acquires rights for Sam Altman biopic Artificial.

Why it matters: Indie film studio Neon has closed a deal to acquire the rights to produce Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s forthcoming $40 million drama about Sam Altman’s leadership of OpenAI, after Amazon unexpectedly abandoned the project despite nearing completion. It comes after Netflix, A24, Mubi, and Focus all chose not to back the film after viewing it at pre-sale screenings, per reports by Variety.

Variety also reported that, according to those who have seen the film — which is set during a tumultuous time at the AI manufacturer, when Altman was fired and then reinstated as CEO in late 2023 — Guadagnino’s portrayal of the executive is less than favorable.

The move reignites questions about Substantial Tech’s growing influence over culture: Amazon’s decision followed its multi-billion-dollar OpenAI partnership, prompting speculation over whether commercial relationships are beginning to shape creative output. The news follows Google’s $75 million investment in indie film studio A24, which experts say was a bet on its creative influence and cultural legitimacy.

The news: “Exuberant” AI spending could threaten the global economy, the Bank for International Settlements warns.

It has been revealed that why it matters: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), often referred to as the central bank for central banks, has warned that Big Tech’s trillion-dollar AI spending spree risks ending in a prolonged investment bust, if the promised returns fail to materialize. In a report published on Sunday, the BIS compared today’s AI race with historical investment booms — from Britain’s railway expansion to the dotcom bubble — and argued that transformative technologies often attract more capital than commercial returns can ultimately justify.

The warning comes as the five largest hyperscaling tech companies — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — are expected to spend more than $1 trillion on AI infrastructure by the end of 2026.

It has been revealed that it’s another reminder that the AI boom is becoming a macroeconomic story that extends beyond the technology sector. Should investment in AI fail to deliver the gains markets are betting on, the resulting slowdown in business confidence and consumer spending would weigh on the entire economy.

The news: L’Oréal and OpenAI announce partnership for AI in beauty product development, content creation, and product discovery.

In a recent development, why it matters: L’Oréal Group has revealed a strategic partnership with OpenAI, marking one of the beauty industry’s most significant moves yet into conversational commerce. Unveiled at the Vivatech conference in Paris, the partnership will explore applications across research, marketing and consumer discovery, while bringing L’Oreal’s brands into ChatGPT, including Maybelline New York. Maybelline will also be part of an experiment into the virtual try-on (VTO) of some beauty products by the two companies.

According to recent reports, L’Oréal stated it will also work with OpenAI to strengthen product discovery within ChatGPT across brands in the US, from Lancôme to Kérastase. Meanwhile, Skinceuticals, Cerave, and Garnier are all part of ChatGPT’s global ad pilot.

It has been revealed that it’s another sign that large fashion and beauty groups are investing in AIO, optimizing for AI assistants that are rapidly emerging as the next discovery layer. Experts are split, however, on whether VTO in beauty is something consumers actually want — some respondents to our Vogue Business AI consumer perception survey remarked it’s a category where influencer recommendations and in-store product testing are preferred.

The news: UK bans access to social media platforms for under-16s.

Why it matters: The UK is banning social media for under-16s, effective next year. Prime Minister Keir Starmer remarked the restrictions will be modeled on those set by the Australian government last December, comprising a ban for the age group on platforms where the “sole and significant purpose” is to facilitate social interaction. This will include Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Reddit, TikTok, X, YouTube and Twitch, likely alongside other platforms such as dating apps and Bluesky. Pinterest, YouTube Kids, and messenger apps like Whatsapp are not included in the ban.

According to recent reports, the UK is going a step further than Australia, however, banning all platforms from offering live streaming to under-16s and prohibiting strangers from making contact with the age group. Gaming platforms like Roblox and Discord — also not included in the blanket ban — will still need to abide by these rules. AI chatbots enabling romantic companionship will be banned for under-18s.

It’s the latest sign that the anti-social media movement is reaching a tipping point, as the push to limit children’s exposure to addictive algorithms and other potential online harms extends beyond activist interests into the mainstream. Brands and marketers will need to adapt their strategies for how they reach these consumers, which will likely result in a much more fragmented marketing space. Experts say multiplayer games like Roblox and Fortnite — where under-16s are socializing more — could become an appealing alternative for brands.

The news: Meta rolls out AI agents for business users in Whatsapp monetization push.

Why it matters: Meta has introduced AI-powered business tools on Whatsapp, launching a Meta business AI agent, designed to handle customer interactions end-to-end — from answering customer queries and booking appointments, to recommending products and closing sales, without the need of a human. It’s one of Meta’s first moves into commercial-facing operations, outside its core advertising business, and unlocks a huge revenue stream for the tech giant as it continues to invest millions in AI.

Many luxury brands already use Whatsapp as an informal clienteling channel, for sales associates to maintain a direct, ongoing relationship with high-value customers. Embedding AI into that environment could allow brands to scale this communication beyond the highest value customers, without the need for hiring human teams. It’s also another sign of Big Tech’s push into conversational commerce.

But as brands look to build closer relationships with customers, the move also positions Meta as the third-party infrastructure layer through which those interactions increasingly flow. What’s more, Whatsapp’s appeal has long been its perception as a more private, encrypted space, but the introduction of AI-generated interactions could shift consumer perception of the space — particularly relevant for the luxury customers who value discretion and trust.

The news: Elon Musk’s SpaceX seeks to raise the world’s largest ever IPO.

In a recent development, why it matters: Elon Musk’s space and AI company SpaceX is seeking to raise as much as $86 billion at a valuation of around $1.8 trillion, in what would be the world’s largest ever IPO, according to an amended IPO filing submitted last Wednesday. SpaceX is now framing itself as an AI infrastructure company as well as a space technology business that makes rockets and satellites, so proceeds from the IPO would go toward both its space and AI computing ambitions.

It comes just a week after Anthropic filed for a Upcoming York IPO with an expected valuation of $1 trillion. Both these valuations upon filing signal just how strongly markets are rewarding companies that can attach themselves to the AI infrastructure story, and points to a broader shift in where influence sits. As capital flows toward AI infrastructure companies, they can gain greater control over access, pricing, and performance — factors that will shape how widely the tech can be deployed across fashion.

The news: Anthropic files for a Fresh York IPO that’s set to value the firm at more than $1 trillion.

Why it matters: Anthropic closed a fresh funding round of $65 billion just last week, announcing a upcoming valuation of $900 billion. The news pitches Anthropic slightly ahead of AI rival OpenAI, which is also planning to file for an IPO. (OpenAI was valued at $852 billion in March, when it raised its last funding round of $122 billion.) These are unprecedented sums of money, even within the Silicon Valley tech world, and signal just how bullish private investors are on the potential of AI.

If public market investors pour money into these companies upon listing, too, then a large part of both public and private capital will be concentrated in the AI sector. This is what some financial experts warn can cause a financial bubble to burst, while others believe the potential of this tech is fairly reflected by these amounts. Anthropic has seen major financial gains in the last year, with annualized revenues (the estimate of annual revenue based on recent performance) increasing fivefold from last year to $47 billion in May.

When startups confidentially file for an IPO, they do so to gauge investor interest — Anthropic could still decide to scrap its aims to go public, if the market is not favorable.

The news: Pope Leo XIV delivers his first encyclical, calling for AI to be regulated and “disarmed”.

Why it matters: Last week, Pope Leo XIV delivered his first encyclical, titled Magnifica Humanitas (“Magnificent Humanity”), and in it, he chose to focus on AI and the future of humanity. The Pope called for AI to be “disarmed”, warning against its use in manipulation, surveillance, and warfare, while urging that its development be guided by human dignity, ethical responsibility, and the common good.

Industry observers note that his decision to focus on AI signals a broader cultural shift: AI is no longer just a technological issue, but a moral and societal one. The speech reflected the growing unease over the pace of technological adoption that can be felt across the world. Brands must now consider that AI governance is being reframed from a commercial responsibility to an ethical one, and as they accelerate investment in AI to improve operations and consumer-facing touchpoints, they should prepare for scrutiny over intent, authorship, and human agency.

The news: Google unveils its first AI smart glasses.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Google’s much-anticipated AI smart glasses have finally landed. Its Intelligent Eyewear range arrives a year after the tech organization confirmed it was working with eyewear groups Warby Parker, Kering Eyewear, and Gentle Monster on a model to rival those of the Meta Ray-Bans. Unveiled on Tuesday, at the annual Google I/O developer conference, the frames were developed in partnership with Samsung, and have built-in speakers, cameras and microphones, so users can listen to music, make calls, and take photos. Google’s AI model, Google Gemini, is integrated within the glasses, to handle live prompts and enable users to look up information about their surroundings, and get live directions or translations.

In a recent development, google and Gentle Monster’s collaborative debut design comes in the form of oval frames, while the Google x Warby Parker model offers a more traditional wayfarer shape in dark green nylon. Both eyewear groups will launch their full Intelligent Eyewear collections this fall, but did not specify how many designs will feature. Gentle Monster’s first collection will include audio glasses, with voice-assisted support coming later in the fall, while Warby Parker’s will feature “multiple” optical and sun styles that work with a broad range of prescriptions and lenses.

According to recent reports, “These glasses give you powerful newly introduced tools, but they’re designed to feel intuitive and unobtrusive, so you can stay focused on the people and moments in front of you,” said Neil Blumenthal, co-founder and co-CEO of Warby Parker. “Every detail and curve was considered for extended, everyday use, from the fit and balance of the frame to enhanced grip and stability.”.

Google’s smart glasses debut comes three years after the Ray-Ban Meta glasses landed. Apple, Snap, Nothing, OpenAI, and Jony Ive’s IO are all expected to release AI smart glasses in the near future. (Read all about where the market stands in our wearables guide here.).

The news: Google debuts Universal Cart AI shopping hub.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Google used its I/O 2026 conference on Tuesday to unveil Universal Cart, an AI-powered shopping hub that represents the most significant shift in e-commerce — from search-based browsing to what the industry calls “agentic commerce” — to date. Built across Google Search, Gemini, YouTube and Gmail, the new feature allows consumers to add products to a single cross-platform cart, while AI models track pricing, surface loyalty rewards, flag compatibility issues between products, and enable shoppers to either “Buy Now” or divert to the merchant’s website to complete their purchase.

Underpinning the launch is Google’s broader push to establish infrastructure for AI-led commerce through its Universal Commerce Protocol and new Agent Payments Protocol, which aim to standardize how AI agents browse, transact, and pay across retailers.

In a recent development, google said its fresh checkout features will soon be available across merchants like Nike, Sephora, Target, Ulta Beauty, Walmart and Wayfair — as well as Shopify merchants, such as Fenty and Steve Madden. In all cases, the brand stays the merchant of record — the company that’s legally responsible for processing the transaction and selling the product to the end customer. Universal Cart will be rolled out across Google Search and the Gemini app in the US this summer, with YouTube and Gmail to follow.

Industry observers note that alongside Alibaba’s recent integration of Qwen AI across Taobao and Tmall, Google’s announcement reinforces how major tech companies are competing to own the AI interface layer between consumers and brands. Rather than simply serving ads or search results, platforms want AI systems that can curate products, manage transactions, and shape purchasing decisions. It’s a shift that could reshape how brands and retailers’ products are discovered online, moving influence away from keywords, storefronts, and traditional e-commerce sites towards AI-mediated recommendation systems.

The news: Google unveils 24-7 agentic AI personal assistant, Gemini Spark.

In a recent development, users will be able to set recurring tasks for Google Gemini Spark, from “automatically parsing monthly credit card statements to flagging new or hidden subscription fees”. Google Gemini Spark can also be directed to check inboxes for ongoing updates from certain senders, extract urgent deadlines, and send a daily digest of email content, as well as parse raw meeting notes across users’ emails and chats, creating polished summaries in Google Docs or drafting emails.

Google is also expanding Gemini AI’s connections with external apps, tools, and data bases — starting with OpenTable, Instacart, and Canva from today. More partners are presently being integrated and will be declared over the summer, the manufacturer remarked.

According to recent reports, “Spark operates under your direction,” Google said in a statement. “You choose whether to turn it on and what apps it connects to, and it’s designed to ask you first before performing high-stakes actions like spending money or sending emails.”.

This is the most significant shift toward agentic AI — broadly defined as models that can autonomously perform end-to-end tasks on behalf of humans — to date. (Read our guide to what it is here.).

The news: Cate Blanchett launches non-profit to protect artists from AI misuse.

Why it matters: Actress and producer Cate Blanchett has debuted a non-profit organization, RSL Media, to develop what it calls a “human consent standard” for artists to formally declare permissions of use for their identity and creative works in a format that AI models can read.

Co-founded with tech executive Nikki Hexum, RSL Media has formulated its latest creative permissions registry to be open access as of June, so that any member of the public can declare AI use permissions to protect their voice, likeness, and creative work.

Actors Javier Bardem, George Clooney, Tom Hanks, Dame Helen Mirren, Meryl Streep, and Emma Thompson are among the stars supporting the initiative, as well as the Creative Artists Agency and the Music Artists Coalition.

Recent findings suggest that “AI technologies are expanding rampantly, essentially unchecked and unregulated. In order for humans to remain in front of these technologies, consent must be the first consideration,” Blanchett remarked in a statement announcing the launch. “RSL Media is a simple, effective, and free solutions-based technology for facilitating and activating consent. It’s also the industry’s first practical solution, where people everywhere, not just public figures, can assert control over how their work is used by AI.”.

The news: Amazon integrates AI into its search bar for US customers.

Why it matters: Amazon is incorporating AI into the search bar of its US website and mobile app via what it’s calling “Alexa for Shopping” — an AI agent that combines its previous bot Rufus with its AI-powered Alexa+ software. Much like frontier chatbots ChatGPT and Google Gemini, the new tool will respond to customers’ natural language queries with product comparisons and suggestions. Amazon said Alexa for Shopping also becomes “more personal and more helpful over time”, based on conversational data, browsing history, and prior purchases.

It has been revealed that “Alexa for Shopping is like having an expert personal shopper who already knows you and remembers your preferences, purchases, and conversations,” Rajiv Mehta, VP of conversational shopping at Amazon, noted, “and carries that knowledge and understanding of you across your phone, laptop, and Echo devices.” It’s the latest sign that retailers are racing to own more of the shopping journey. Hosting the journey from initial purchase query all the way through the discovery process arms Amazon with more data to power its advertising business and refine operations like inventory management.

The news: Alibaba integrates its Qwen AI within Taobao and Tmall.

Why it matters: Alibaba Group’s decision to integrate its Qwen AI assistant across the entirety of Taobao and Tmall’s marketplaces — spanning roughly four billion products across consumer-to-consumer (Taobao) and business-to-business (Tmall) — offers one of the clearest indications that China is moving fast in turning generative AI into a mainstream consumer shopping behavior.

It has been revealed that qwen is Alibaba’s family of AI models (similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT), which functions as both a chatbot and an AI operating layer across the Alibaba ecosystem. The group rolled out the Qwen app in November 2025, racking up 100 million active monthly customers by January 2026. Alibaba is now embedding Qwen directly into its e-commerce infrastructure, so that users can search conversationally, compare products, receive styling suggestions, track pricing, access virtual try-ons, and complete purchases without leaving the interface.

The news: Meta adds AI-powered visual recognition of children and teens.

Why it matters: Just over a month since Meta was held liable in a landmark US legal case that found its algorithms designed to be addictive for children and teens, the tech giant has revealed it will begin using AI to scan photos and videos of owners for visual clues of whether they are under 13 and should be removed from the social platforms.

In a recent development, “We want to be clear: this is not facial recognition,” Meta explained in a blog post. “Our AI looks at general themes and visual cues, for example height or bone structure, to estimate someone’s general age; it does not identify the specific person in the image. By combining these visual insights with our analysis of text and interactions, we can significantly increase the number of underage accounts we identify and remove.”.

It’s a move that might affect fashion brands reliant on Meta’s ecosystems for ad marketing and growth, while this new AI tool specifically poses another sign of just how swiftly AI is becoming embedded within the infrastructure of social platforms, often in ways that consumers barely even notice.

In a recent development, one of the biggest criticisms of AI’s applications for more creative pursuits is the question of creative IP — as it stands, frontier AI models were initially trained more like open extraction systems than licensed commercial ones, which has led to some artists and photographers, for example, having their work pirated. As AI tools become particularly embedded in marketing, e-commerce, and content production, the provenance of training data has become a central industry tension. The outcome of cases like this will help shape how creative content is valued online in the AI era.

The news: Big Tech’s AI spending prepares swell to $725 billion for 2026.

In a recent development, why it matters: Big Tech’s big four — Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google parent company Alphabet — reported their Q1 earnings yesterday, each raising their AI infrastructure spending aims once again. This time, to $725 billion between them — up 77% from their combined record capital expenditures of $410 billion in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft is planning up to $190 billion in capital expenditures, up from analysts’ forecast of $152 billion; Meta raised its spending to between $125 billion and $145 billion, a massive jump from its $72 billion last year; and Amazon defended its $200 billion investment plans. Alphabet was the standout performer, thanks to 63% revenue growth from Google Cloud, which Google CEO Sundar Pichai credited to demand for its enterprise AI products. Meta’s shares, on the other hand, sank 10% in Thursday trading, despite beating expectations on revenue and profit, which analysts believe was down to investor nervousness around its massive increase in spending, before AI’s promises are realized.

It has been revealed that all this had analysts saying the AI bubble indicates no signs of bursting soon — but it’s clear there’s a mismatch between the large scale of AI spending and the incremental revenue gains it’s facilitating so far. Despite reporting strong revenues, Significant Tech’s margins are increasingly under pressure. The effects of this AI spending push were particularly clear at Amazon, where free cash flow plummeted 95% to $1.2 billion in the last 12 months.

The news: OpenAI releases new image generator, ChatGPT Images 2.0.

According to recent reports, why it matters: It’s an upgraded version of ChatGPT’s image-generating tool — used by thousands of consumers and businesses worldwide — and comes a month after the tech company wound down its video-generation tool, Sora. OpenAI indicates Images 2.0 has several expanded capabilities and higher quality output. It can generate 10 images at a time and handle much longer prompts than before — paragraphs instead of minimal word prompts, according to OpenAI — as well as possessing apparent “thinking capabilities” to “double check” outputs.

It’s also designed to be better at crawling the internet for visual references to create higher quality mockups of magazines, manga, and other creative work. “Its sense of composition and visual taste means results feel less AI-generated and more intentionally designed,” OpenAI mentioned in a blog post announcing the release.

Photographers and creative agencies fear a world where clients go straight to tools like Images 2.0 to save resources and time, with the upgraded generator able to parse visual references that were posted to the internet as recently as December 2025 — a factor that will likely intensify concerns around AI’s immediate reproduction of their creative IP.

The news: Meta to cut 10% of workforce “to offset” investments in AI.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Meta will lay off 10% of its workforce — around 8,000 employees — next month, in a move designed to offset its aggressive spending on AI. The tech firm told staff in an internal memo that it was making the staff cuts in order to “run the company more efficiently and [...] offset the other investments we’re making”. A spokesperson for Meta confirmed the news. It comes after chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said Meta will increase its spending as much as almost double this year, to $135 billion.

According to recent reports, this AI funding signals just how bullish tech companies are on the promise of the rapidly developing tech. Meta’s share price has been volatile since the firm declared these spending hikes, signaling that investors still don’t know where they stand. (Here’s a recap of what the AI bubble burst would mean for fashion.).

The news: Anthropic follows OpenAI with UK office expansion aims.

Why it matters: Anthropic has leased a new London office that will have enough space for 800 employees — roughly four times its current headcount in the British capital. The new 158,000-square-foot space is located in King Cross, the same neighborhood where OpenAI will open its first permanent office in London in 2027, with capacity for 544 employees.
