📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brigadeiros are like a cross between fudge and Tootsie Rolls in truffle form.
  • As a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form.
  • Brigadeiros start with a can of sweetened condensed milk, plus cocoa powder and butter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Brigadeiros are like a cross between fudge and Tootsie Rolls in truffle form. They're easy to make at home, and even easier to pop in your mouth.

As a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form. Brigadeiros have the familiar flavor and fudgy center of a really good chocolate truffle, but they’re even easier to make because they don’t require melting any chocolate. Everything happens in one small saucepan, and the only difficult part is waiting for the mixture to chill.

Brigadeiros start with a can of sweetened condensed milk, plus cocoa powder and butter. The butter is key to carrying the flavor of the cocoa powder and giving the bite-sized treats their signature soft bite. They end up as glossy little chocolate balls covered in sprinkles that taste halfway between a chocolate truffle and a piece of fudge: dense and chewy with a deep cocoa flavor and a center so creamy it nearly melts on contact.

It has been revealed that brigadeiros are Brazilian confections made by cooking a mixture of sweetened condensed milk, cocoa and butter until it’s thick. Once cooled, the mixture is rolled into bite-size balls. A Brazilian birthday party isn’t complete without a tray of brigadeiros, but they also show up at weddings, baby showers and holiday gatherings. Some cooks skip the rolling altogether and eat the soft mixture with a spoon, a style called brigadeiro de colher.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a small saucepan, combine the sweetened condensed milk, cocoa powder and butter. Cook, stirring constantly, on medium-low heat until the mixture is thickened, 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer the mixture to a medium bowl. Refrigerate it, covered, for two hours or until it’s firm enough to be rolled.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Shape the chilled mixture into 1-inch balls. Roll the balls in chocolate sprinkles.

Sources indicate that editor’s Tip: Rub a little butter on your palms before rolling, and grease them again every few balls. This will keep the mixture from sticking and give each truffle a smooth surface.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Keep brigadeiros in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Store them in paper candy cups or in a single layer separated by parchment so they don’t stick together. Cold brigadeiros get firm, so let them sit out for about 15 minutes before serving to bring back their soft, fudgy centers.

Brigadeiros last up to one week in an airtight container in the refrigerator. They taste best within the first few days while the sprinkles are still crisp.

Yes, you can make brigadeiros ahead of time. Cook the chocolate mixture up to two days in advance and keep it covered in the refrigerator, then roll and coat the truffles the day you blueprint to serve them. If the mixture is too stiff to scoop, let it stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes.

Yes, brigadeiros freeze well. Arrange the rolled truffles on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them until they’re firm, about one hour, then transfer them to an airtight container and freeze them for up to three months. Thaw them overnight in the refrigerator.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a recent development, when the brigadeiro mixture stays soft and sticky even after chilling, it almost always means that it needs more time on the stove. Scrape it back into the saucepan and cook it over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for a few more minutes until it thickens and pulls away from the bottom of the pan in one mass. Watch the mixture closely because overcooking will turn it stiff and grainy.

It has been revealed that no, brigadeiros won’t work with regular milk. Brigadeiros depend on the concentrated sugar and milk solids in sweetened condensed milk to cook down into a thick fudge that can be rolled. If you’re out of it, you can make your own sweetened condensed milk by simmering whole milk and sugar until the mixture reduces by about half.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • It has been revealed that it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

It has been revealed that it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

Recent findings suggest that while this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

But getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

It has been revealed that this is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an key role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

Sources indicate that I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

In a recent development, but for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

According to recent reports, smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any fresh bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., mentioned in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

It has been revealed that “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At concern in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

Industry observers note that the Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

According to recent reports, jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, remarked that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He stated the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A newly introduced Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

  • Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

In a recent development, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Industry observers note that making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a significant party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Recent findings suggest that this is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

It has been revealed that dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with major flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

It has been revealed that I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

According to recent reports, the recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

Whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Industry observers note that transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks.
  • Sources indicate that now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party.

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Sources indicate that now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

According to recent reports, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

According to recent reports, I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Sources indicate that meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development.

It has been revealed that the French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for New Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

It has been revealed that as the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content.

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer.

There are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor.

It has been revealed that several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director.

#180361. Latest Update: 57 Food Gifts We’re Giving (and Secretly Hoping to Get) in 2026

Latest Update: 57 Food Gifts We’re Giving (and Secretly Hoping to Get) in 2026

📅 24 Nov 2023 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s never too early to get a head start on holiday gifting.
  • It has been revealed that A handmade mug is a little luxury they’ll use every day (and think of you when they do!).
  • It has been revealed that I recently added these elegant tumblers to my collection thinking they’d be great for dinner parties, and they are—but they’ve also become my fresh favorite everyday water and iced latte glasses, because while they’re beautiful, they feel sturdy enough for daily use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s never too early to get a head start on holiday gifting. After all, getting your shopping done now means you can focus on the important things once the holidays actually roll around—you know, like spending time with family, cooking a festive feast, and enjoying plenty of mulled cider and wine. If you’re in need of gifts for the food people in your life, look no further. These are the 57 gifts we’re planning to give (or hoping to receive) this year.

It has been revealed that A handmade mug is a little luxury they’ll use every day (and think of you when they do!). Tailor your pick to your giftee’s caffeine preferences to make it feel more personal: opt for an oversized mug for the friend who needs drip coffee on an IV, or a more petite cup for the cappuccino drinker.

It has been revealed that I recently added these elegant tumblers to my collection thinking they’d be great for dinner parties, and they are—but they’ve also become my fresh favorite everyday water and iced latte glasses, because while they’re beautiful, they feel sturdy enough for daily use. They bring a smile to my face every time I use them, which is exactly what a great gift should do, isn’t it?

An olive oil can is the kind of thing that’s meant to live on your counter, so why not upgrade to a beautiful one? This sleek stainless-steel model from Seattle-based design studio Holcomb has been in my gifting rotation since it was released. It goes with multiple different home aesthetics and looks equally at home by the stove as it does on a dinner party table.

Industry observers note that give the designated host friend a set of whimsical spiral-tipped serving utensils to use at their next dinner party. And don’t worry, they’re dishwasher-safe.

Buttered toast is a perfect food, in my opinion, and anyone that agrees will adore this handblown glass butter keeper from East Fork. Its design ensures your butter can be kept at room temperature for weeks without spoiling, which means it’ll stay perfectly spreadable and ready to be swiped across whatever carbs you choose.

Any friend who cooks will appreciate receiving this set of ramekins from cult-favorite pottery brand East Fork. At four ounces, they’re a versatile size that works for equally as well for portioning mise en place as it does for serving condiments or sauces.

It has been revealed that this stylish pepper grinder looks incredibly cool, but it’s also made with function in mind. That swanky-looking handle? It’s designed to be ergonomic, able to be held and twisted in myriad ways depending on what’s most comfortable for the user. This gift set pairs the grinder with Piper’s 50-50 blend of black and red peppercorns, portioned into four individual packets to ensure the spices stay fresh.

Sidekick End Grain Cutting Board.

Recent findings suggest that these stunning wood cutting boards are truly heirloom-worthy, handcrafted by expert woodworkers from sturdy hardwood. They’re versatile pieces that are durable enough to be your everyday chopping boards and beautiful enough to serve as serving vessels for cheese and charcuterie.

Recent findings suggest that you can’t go wrong with a beautiful vase, especially if you fill that vase with a bouquet of fresh flowers. This colorful glass number is sure to earn your giftee compliments, and I love that it’s hand-blown, which means every piece is one-of-a-kind.

It has been revealed that you never know when you need a large bowl until you find yourself in need of a large bowl. Any person who likes to host should have a few attractive options on hand, and a splatter enamelware bowl is a pretty timeless choice.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun newly introduced seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

In a recent development, the next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

Get the friend who nerds out on coffee roasting and fermentation processes a subscription to Podium Coffee Club’s Platinum tier, which sources its monthly beans from award-winning roasters across the country. The Platinum tier is focused on rare coffee varietals made using experimental techniques, so it’s perfect for someone who likes an expressive, unique roast.

This gift set brings a taste of Richard Christiansen’s Flamingo Estate to your pantry. It’s full of high-quality products you’ll actually use—no weird spice blends or waxy chocolates here.

It has been revealed that for the friend who would gladly eat tinned fish for dinner every night, I suggest this 10-pack of greatest hits from Fishwife. It’s got a little bit of everything, from the brand’s smoked salmon collab with Fly By Jing to the fan-favorite Smoked Rainbow Trout with Chimichurri, plus limited edition Little Sardines, which are available only as a part of holiday sets.

We all know someone who finishes every dish with flaky salt. Get them this pack of tins from Jacobsen Salt Co., each of which is filled with a different kind of infused salt. They’re small enough to slip into even the tiniest of purses, so your salt-loving friend will never be without their favorite flaky finisher.

When in doubt, opt for wine. But instead of picking up a random bottle, treat your giftee to a month (or three or six!) of deliveries from New York City wine bar and shop Parcelle, whose Wine Drop subscription service has been a longtime BA fave. Choose between red, white, rare, or a curated monthly mix, and Parcelle will take care of the rest.

If you know somebody with a matcha habit that’s burning a hole through their wallet, they’d probably appreciate a set of ceremonial-grade powders from a tried-and-true brand like Matchaful. This set is also perfect for demonstrating just how different matcha powders can be.

This snazzy supply of olive oil is a great example of a practical item that’s still gift-worthy. The bold tin (designed in collaboration with Los Angeles–based artist Dave Bowers) makes it a statement kitchen decor piece, and the oil inside is cold-pressed in California by one of our favorite olive oil brands.

Recent findings suggest that diaspora Spice Co. spices are nothing like the bottles you'd find at the grocery store. Do a side by side smell test and the difference will be obvious to you. Diaspora’s product offerings have expanded quite a bit since it first got going. If the choices are overwhelming, the brand’s gift sets, like this one assembled by the one and only Padma Lakshmi, is a no-fail choice.

Balsamic Vinegar of Modena & White Condiment Set.

Not all balsamic vinegars are created equally. Giusti is one of the oldest names in the business, and its vinegars are truly exceptional. The three medal is the brand’s most popular bottle, striking an ideal balance between sweetness and acidity. The white condiment is light and zippy and, honestly, good enough to drink.

Recent findings suggest that this marmalade is the closest thing you can get to spreading Ojai, California on your morning toast. The flavors aren’t typical of marmalades you’d find in the store, the brand accents that bittersweet citrus zing with hibiscus and honey. Their fruit spreads are fantastic too.

According to recent reports, you'd be pretty hard-pressed to find a cast-iron skillet like the Field No.5. Its sloped edges make tossing and flipping ingredients like a chef very easy, something you most definitely can’t do with your standard Lodge. Senior editor Olivia Tarantino uses hers every time she makes eggs.

According to recent reports, fellow’s full suite of cocktail-making tools looks like they’d fit right in among the equipment inside a spaceship laboratory (in the best possible way). It includes a jigger, a glass mixing vessel, a cocktail shaker, two strainers, a muddler, a bar spoon, and a tray to keep it all together.

Food storage is about as practical as gifts get, but Misenware makes it feel special. Our testing samples vanished from the BA office almost instantly, and plenty of staffers bought their own once we had run out. The stainless-steel containers seal so tightly that we have no fear of soup leaking in a work bag. They’re microwave-safe, they won’t stain, and they held up when we jumped up and down on them. A universal lid fits every size, and each piece nests inside the next. This Gear of the Year winner has never been on sale, so grab a set to give and another to keep while it's 25% off.

These cheery yellow kitchen scissors aren’t just fun to look at—they’re super practical too. The shears come equipped with a bottle opener, a nutcracker, and a lid opener, and the blades separate for easy cleaning, plus the bright color makes them easy to spot amid all your other cooking tools.

In a recent development, that aunt who always insists on baking the pies for Thanksgiving? Get her a handmade walnut rolling pin she’ll use for years to come. These French-style pins come in a marbled cardboard case that’s perfect for gifting. Their handleless design makes them comfortable to grip and easy to maneuver, and allows you to get a nuanced feel for your dough as you roll.

Tawashi Little Fish Dishcloths, Set of 2.

In a recent development, these adorable scrubbers are great for cleaning grime off delicate cookware, dishes, or glassware. They’re absorbent and fast-drying, and they have hooks for hanging—plus they’re incredibly cute.

This tortoise-handled bottle opener from Parisian flatware brand Sabre makes for a handsome host gift, especially when paired with a bottle of your favorite pét-nat or non-alc apéritif.

Sources indicate that I’m secretly hoping someone restocks my own supply of this luxurious hand wash this holiday season. It comes in a glass bottle that’s so pretty I took to refilling it with cheaper hand soap after the original soap was long gone, but the scent—a delicate mix of jasmine, geranium, and orange blossom—is what really makes it worth buying.

These all-natural firestarters are a chic alternative to the typical firestarter logs, and they’d make an excellent host gift for the friend who’s lucky enough to have a fireplace or outdoor fire pit.

Give the gift of cozy hot pot nights at home with this cute and compact appliance by Fly By Jing. You could even pair it with an H Mart gift card so your giftee can stock up on thinly sliced meats and other add-ins.

Profile Opal Mini Nugget Ice Maker.

Sources indicate that the iced beverage fiend in your life will go gaga for this mini version of our longtime favorite ice maker, the GE Opal. Despite its more compact footprint and lower price tag, it produces the same crunchy nugget ice we know and love—and it’s available in some cute colorways.

Give the latte lover who also values convenience this do-it-all machine from Nespresso, which combines the brand’s signature pod technology with an automatic milk frother that’ll have them pouring latte art like a pro.

Recent findings suggest that cookbooks make for great gifts, and lucky for you, we’ve spent all year cooking through dozens of them to find the best ones. These are a few favorites from our quarterly best upcoming releases roundups, like Yotam Ottolenghi’s latest collection of weeknight-friendly recipes and Roxana Jullapat’s ode to morning baking.

Obsessed With the Best: 100+ Methodically Perfected Recipes Based on 20+ Head-to-Head Tests.

Ohana Style: Food from Hawai'i, for Your Family.

In a recent development, no. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World: At-Home Recipes from the Streets, Truck Stops, Villages, and Palaces of India.

Hello, Home Cooking: Do-Able Dishes for Every Day.

Morning Baker: Recipes and Rituals for Breakfast and Beyond.

It has been revealed that former BA staffer Ali Francis teamed up with illustrator Adriana Picker to create a truly one-of-a-kind book about the fascinating histories of vegetables. It’s truly a gem to behold, and the sort of book any cooking enthusiast would find joy in. Also, each year Phaidon complications a spectacular array of beautifully crafted and often massive cookbooks and tomes on food.

The Curious Lives of Vegetables: An Artful Exploration of the Wonderful World of Edible Plants, Their History, and Their Crucial Role in Our Future by Ali Francis.

Le Cordon Bleu Culinary Arts School: Volumes 1-7 by André Cointreau.

The Festive Baker: A Cookbook - Baking for celebrations and special occasions around the world by Ben Mervis.

The Photographer's Cookbook by Lisa Hostetler.
